set.hook: Christophe Quéant's starred market kitchen on Place Carnot, three-course lunch at 50 €.
set.why: The house is old and the façade modern; inside, MICHELIN describes a beige room of exposed stone a short walk from the Hôtel-Dieu. Christophe Quéant came through the Robuchon and Ducasse kitchens and cooks seasonal plates on classical foundations. Gault&Millau's 2026 review tasted foie gras with langoustines and artichoke, lobster salad with tarragon and romesco, and a verbena soufflé with grapefruit sorbet. In the evening the shortest of the three menus is called Petit Pasumot.
set.verdict: The MICHELIN page still shows one star after the 2026 selection, and Gault&Millau 2026 gives 13/20, calling the cooking bourgeois and regional, technically sure. Lunch at 50 € is the sensible way in; dinner climbs to 178 €. Diners' reviews note tables set close together and some noise, and one called the sole and the soufflé the high points of an otherwise uneven six courses.

set.caveat: Closed Sunday and Monday, no Tuesday lunch; book, the room is small and the tables close

set.hook: Jordan Billan's starred dining room in a wine merchant's manor on the ring boulevard.
set.why: MICHELIN describes the building as a winegrower's manor on Boulevard Maréchal-Foch, with tables moved into the garden in summer; the cedar on the lawn gives the hotel and the restaurant their name. Jordan Billan cooks from Burgundian suppliers he names, and the plates run from matured Charolais beef with bone marrow to sole with shellfish and a kasha risotto. Gault&Millau's 2026 entry puts the bill at 95 to 190 € a head before wine.
set.verdict: The star dates from the 2022 guide (Yonder) and is still on the MICHELIN page after the 2026 selection. This is the more formal of Beaune's two starred rooms and the one that runs lunch at the weekend, which makes it the safer Sunday booking during the auction. Expect hotel-restaurant polish rather than surprise, and prices to match.

set.hook: Mikihiko Sawahata grills beef and eel over binchotan at a ten-seat counter on rue Maufoux.
set.why: About ten stools face the grill, so the meal is watched as much as eaten. Mikihiko Sawahata's speciality is sumibi-yaki over Japanese binchotan: Miyazaki wagyu, or Limousin beef aged 40 days, or fish. Gault&Millau's 2026 entry adds sushi, tempura, eel and beef tongue off the charcoal. Sachiko, his wife and co-owner, runs a sake and wine list that Jancis Robinson found long on lesser-known Burgundy at fair prices, and young growers eat here.
set.verdict: Gault&Millau selected it for 2026 at 45 to 63 € a head before drinks, well under the starred tables, and the crowd of local winemakers says more than any guide. Reviews disagree on the food: some find the produce and tempura exact, others call portions thin. Go for the grill and the bottles, sit at the counter, and book: ten seats fill.

set.hook: The Escoffier family's 1996 bistro off Place Carnot, now a sharing-plate wine room under the son.
set.why: Pierre and Fabienne Escoffier opened Ma Cuisine in 1996 in a former bookshop down the passage Sainte-Hélène, and it became the table where the wine trade ate oeufs en meurette and pigeon with bottles from a deep cellar. Their son Mathieu, who also took the name to Singapore in 2018, now runs it. Gault&Millau's 2026 review describes a looser room built for sharing: prawns, pata negra, Galician beef, a regional cellar, very little by the glass.
set.verdict: Treat it as a call-first address this year. Gault&Millau's 2026 review (12/20) describes a working dinner room, but MICHELIN's page carries an undated 'temporarily closed' notice, and the February 2026 reopening in our old record was not found. If it is open, go for the cellar and a late booking; do not promise guests the old canon menu.

set.hook: Wine bar and bistro on pedestrian rue Monge: oeufs en meurette, bourguignon, 600 bottles.
set.why: A small bistro and wine bar on a pedestrian street off Place Monge, with a terrace outside and Mickael Thibert in the kitchen. The plates are the ones Burgundy is known for: eggs poached in red wine with lardons, beef braised for hours, and a fish of the day. The list is the surprise for the size of the room: more than 600 references by Gault&Millau's count, more than 500 by the tourist office's.
set.verdict: Gault&Millau keeps it in its 2026 selection at about 45 € a head before wine, which is honest money for the canon cooked properly. Reviewers say it fills fast and to come early if you have not booked. It is the straight answer to a guest who wants bourguignon in Beaune without the tourist-menu version.

set.hook: Romain Escoffier's Bib Gourmand on Boulevard Foch, the menu rewritten every fortnight.
set.why: The carte and the set menu drawn from it change every two weeks, and MICHELIN singles out the lamb from the Ferme de Clavisy as the kind of local produce Romain Escoffier builds on. Diners come back for the lamb confit and the desserts, and for a sommelier working a cellar MICHELIN puts at about 800 references. Gault&Millau rates it 12/20, a Table Gourmande, at 27 to 37 € a head before wine.
set.verdict: The best-value serious cooking on the boulevard, and the Bib on its MICHELIN page and in the 2026 tourist office listing backs that. Reviews also report a cool welcome and a strict booking policy, including a 66 € charge for cancelling inside twelve hours. Book ahead for Fridays and weekends, and confirm the penalty when you do.

set.hook: A cave à manger on the Faubourg Madeleine: shelves of bottles, one long shared table, a farm-sourced kitchen.
set.why: The room is a wine shop first: bottles line the walls and diners sit at a long communal table, choosing from the shelves. Le Fooding calls it a cave à manger with a long list and a seasonal menu. In the kitchen Martial Blanchon buys from local growers and farmers, and MICHELIN's example plate is warm potatoes with haddock and a tarragon sabayon: plain things, cooked with punch, to set against a serious bottle.
set.verdict: Gault&Millau 2026 gives it 12/20 and lists a six-course menu at 69 euros built from the carte; MICHELIN keeps it in the selection at €€ with no star or Bib. It is the most solid of the Madeleine wine rooms for a guest who wants the bottle and the plate to carry equal weight. Hours differ by source, so call before promising a day.

set.hook: Pépita Del Rosario's natural-wine épicerie and bistrot on the Faubourg Madeleine, trading since 1996.
set.why: Pépita Del Rosario and Richard Grocat opened the Comptoir in 1996 as an épicerie and cave à manger, seeking out small farmers and winemakers who refuse chemical shortcuts, years before natural wine had a following in Beaune. During lockdown the shop side grew into a fuller épicerie and wine shop. The plates are built from what sits on the shelves and from seasonal, organic-leaning produce; reviewers keep returning to the take-away wine list.
set.verdict: A Raisin visitor in mid-2026 praises the list and Pépita herself, so the house trades; whether the table service runs as it once did is less clear, since Raisin and Le Fooding now file it as a shop and TripAdvisor flags it closed. Treat it as a natural-wine cellar first, call to ask about a table, and expect conviction over polish: some reviewers find the service rough.

set.hook: Natural-wine shop and bar off Place Carnot; an open kitchen does bao and shared plates late in the week.
set.why: Enstase opened as a company in September 2021 and works as three things at once: a cellar of natural, organic and biodynamic bottles (some 900 references from small estates, by its own listing), a bar, and a kitchen. Raisin's 2023 feature describes a cooking station that opens two evenings a week for shared plates and street-food bao. Beyond the wine there are ciders, kefirs, kombuchas and juices, which makes it the one counter in town for a guest off alcohol.
set.verdict: The most recent dated evidence is a set of Raisin visitor comments from October 2025; nothing dated 2026 turned up, and listings disagree on which evenings the kitchen runs. It is still the natural-wine counter of central Beaune on paper. Send nobody without a call or a look at its own channels the same week.
set.signature: Bao and small plates from the open kitchen, with a glass of natural wine
set.caveat: Kitchen only on some evenings (Thu-Fri in 2023, later listings say Thu-Sat or longer); no 2026 evidence: call first

set.hook: Beaune's Saturday morning market, under the covered halles and out across Place Fleury.
set.why: On Saturday morning the stalls fill the covered halles on Place de la Halle and spill across Place Fleury: hill-village producers with Époisses and Cîteaux, slabs of jambon persillé, honey, flowers, and in autumn the first wild mushrooms. The same halles host the Hospices wine auction each November, so the market stands where Burgundy sells its most famous barrels. Wednesday brings a smaller food-only market to the same square.
set.verdict: The Office de Tourisme lists it every Saturday from 1 August to 26 December 2026, 08:00-12:00, which is shorter than the 07:00-13:00 our old record gave. Come early for the producers. On auction weekend the halles are the sale room, and no source says whether Saturday 14 November runs as normal, so check with the tourist office before sending guests.
set.signature: A wedge of Époisses and a slice of jambon persillé, bought from the producers before 10:00
set.caveat: 08:00-12:00 per the tourist office; Saturday 14 Nov (auction weekend) not confirmed; cash useful at small stalls

set.hook: Eddy Raillard's charcuterie at 4 rue Monge: jambon persillé, pâté en croûte and boudin blanc over the counter.
set.why: Eddy Raillard, a charcutier from Le Creusot who trained at Bize in Savigny-lès-Beaune, fills his counter on rue Monge with the Burgundian repertoire: jambon persillé set in its green parsley jelly, pâté en croûte, terrine de campagne, boudin blanc, rosette and dry saucisson, and snails in parsley butter. A queue forms on busy mornings. Buy a thick slice and bread nearby and lunch is done standing up.
set.verdict: The shop exists at 4 rue Monge in public listings and a 2025 review, and Pudlowski called the jambon persillé a model of the genre in 2018, but nothing dated 2026 turned up and the hours on record are from 2018. Reviews praise the pâté en croûte and the persillé and grumble about the welcome. Call before you plan a lunch on it.
set.signature: A thick slice of jambon persillé, with bread and a cornichon
set.caveat: Closed Sunday and Monday morning in 2018; two phone numbers in circulation; reviews mention a brusque welcome and a queue

set.hook: A former Park Hyatt pastry chef's shop on rue Monge: cheesecake, Saint-Honoré, chocolates, a small tea room.
set.why: Fabien Berteau was Gault&Millau's pastry chef of the year in 2015, working beside Jean-François Rouquette at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where his cheesecakes were the signature. He then opened his own shop on rue Monge, a short walk from the Hospices. The counter runs from entremets and red-fruit tarts to bonbons de chocolat, and the cheesecake came with him; a small salon de thé lets you eat the cake on the spot.
set.verdict: Gault&Millau keeps him in its artisan listing and directory pages were updated in February 2026, but no review or post dated 2026 surfaced, so trading is likely rather than proven. The pastry is the reason to go; several reviewers find the service cool. The Sunday-morning opening makes it one of the few good stops on auction Sunday.
set.signature: The cheesecake, the dish he brought from the Park Hyatt
set.caveat: Closed Wednesday; Sunday mornings only; reviews mention cool, slow service
